Chemoselective Reduction
Electrochemical Reduction of α-Amino Allenylphosphonates to
α-Amino Allylphosphonates
Pauline Adler,[a] Pedro de Oliveira,* [b] and Nicolas Rabasso* [a]
In memory of François Couty
Abstract: α-Amino allenylphosphonates are reduced to α-
amino allylphosphonates using electrochemical processes. The
reduction products are obtained in moderate to good yields.
Moreover, in the case of tosylamine compounds, we were
Introduction
Due to their easiness of preparation through the Kabachnik–
Fields reaction,
[1,2] α-aminophosphonates have been exten-
sively studied. [3] The latter exhibit a wide range of biological
activities such as enzyme inhibition or antibactericidal. [4] Over
the past few years we have been interested in the synthesis [5]
and reactivity [6,7] of α-amino allenylphosphonates (AAP) 1.I n
particular, in 2013, we have reported the chemo- and stereo-
selective reduction of α-AAPs 1 to α-amino vinylphosphonates
3 using H
2 and poisoned palladium catalyst (Scheme 1). [8] Our
investigations in this field led us to postulate that the stereo-
selectivity of this reduction depends on the substitution pattern
on the allenyl moiety whereas the chemoselectivity is due to
the preferred reduction of the electron-richer, and in that case
less hindered, double bond of the α-AAP 1. Continuing our
investigations in this field, we now report the chemoselec-
tive reduction of the same α-APPs 1 to prepare the correspond-
ing α-amino allylphosphonates 2 using electrochemistry
(Scheme 1).
Although the reduction of allenylphosphonates to vinylphos-
phonates is well documented using hydrogen and poisoned
catalyst,
[9,10] to date only one case of partial reduction of
allenylphosphonates to allylphosphonates has been reported in
the literature using ammonium formate and Pd catalyst.
[11] In

pleased to take advantage of a simultaneous reduction and
cleavage of the tosyl group from the nitrogen atom to access
unprotected amino-allylphosphonates. The mechanism of this
reduction is also discussed.
Scheme 1. Reduction of allenylphosphonates to vinyl- or allylphosphonates.
the case of α-amino allylphosphonates, after hydrolysis/trans-
formation to the corresponding α-amino allylphosphonic acids,
these compounds could be incorporated to peptides to induce
antimicrobial properties.
[12,13] To date the classical methods for
the synthesis of α-amino allylphosphonates are based on a
Kabachnik–Fields reaction followed by elimination. [14,15] A dif-
ferent strategy based on an aza-Wittig reaction was reported
by Palacios and co-workers in 2007.
[16] More recently, Zhang
and co-workers have prepared allylphosphonates from a cop-
per(I)-catalysed cyclopropene ring opening reaction.
[17]
The common methods for the partial reduction of allenes
involve the use of hydrogen with poisoned catalyst, [8–10]
sodium in liquid ammonia to favour the E isomer[18] or in situ
generated diimide,[19] the last ones having failed to reduce our
substrates.[8] In this context, electrochemistry has been known
for a long time to be efficient for the reduction of allenes. [20,21]
The mechanism of such reduction has been studied as well. [22]
More generally, there are several electrochemical methods well-
known to oxidise and reduce organic compounds efficiently.
[23]
Electrochemistry has been defined by Frontana-Uribe and co-
workers as a process that relates to 9 of the 12 principles of
green chemistry by being clean, environmentally friendly and
scalable to industrial level.
[24] In the context of developing new
selective transformations, we propose here to replace conven-
tional reagents used in organic chemistry with electrodes in
order to explore the electrolysis of α-amino allenylphosphon-
ates 1 to obtain α-amino allylphosphonates 2.

Results and Discussion
For the optimisation of this electrochemical reduction, we
started our investigation with the easily prepared α-AAP 4
(Table 1).[5] We selected acetonitrile as the solvent and Et 4NBF4
as the supporting electrolyte due to their easiness of separation
from the expected product. It has to be noted that other sup-
porting electrolytes such as nBu
4NClO4 and LiClO4 were investi-
gated as well; however, in that case the obtained results were
less conclusive. First, we started to record the cyclic voltammo-
gram for the α-AAP 4 (see Supporting Information). The reduc-
tion potential for the electrolysis was set to –2.50 V, slightly
more negative than the peak potential of the reduction wave.
Next, we turned our attention to the source of protons needed
for this reduction. Although it has been known that the chosen
electrolyte (Et
4NBF4) could decompose during the electrolysis
through a Hofmann type elimination to provide a proton and
a molecule of ethylene,
[21] we noticed in our case a longer reac-
tion time along with the formation of multiple by-products
leading to a more complicated separation of the expected α-
amino allylphosphonate ( α-AAllylP). Although the yield of for-
mation of the α-AAllylP 5 is good in pure acetonitrile with no
external source of protons (66 %), other products, under the
same conditions, were obtained in a lower yield [see com-
pounds 14 (55 %, Scheme 3), 16 (35 %, Scheme 4), 17 (37 %,
Scheme 4), 28 (52 %, Scheme 6) and 33 (45 %, Scheme 6)].
Hence, we investigated different external proton sources
(Table 1, entries 2–5) to conclude that in all cases the reaction
is faster and cleaner than with the supporting electrolyte alone.
The best results for the reduction of the α-AAP 4 to the α-
AAllylP 5 were observed with phenol and diethyl malonate. The
latter is electro-inactive and gives the best result in terms of
reproducibility. Indeed, the use of succinimide (entry 2) pro-
vides the desired allylphosphonate 5 along with multiple by-
products, whereas benzoic acid (entry 4), a stronger acid, leads
to a low conversion of 4 to 5. Moreover, the use of phenol
(entry 3) is not recommended due to its toxicity and to the fact
that traces of the latter are recovered in the final product.
Table 1. Optimisation of the reaction conditions: proton source.
[a] Isolated yield obtained from the reduction of 4 in a 1:1 mixture of CH 3CN
and DMF .
Although acetonitrile seems to be a good solvent for this
reaction, we had some reproducibility problems as well as for-
mation of multiple unidentified by-products, probably resulting
Eur. J. Org. Chem. 2020, 3918–3925 www.eurjoc.org © 2020 Wiley-VCH Verlag GmbH & Co. KGaA, Weinheim3919
from the decomposition of the starting material. By switching
the solvent from acetonitrile to DMF we observed a more repro-
ducible and cleaner reaction. In contrast with acetonitrile, in
DMF, without any external source of protons, the conversion of
the α-AAP 4 to the α-AAllylP 5 is incomplete and much longer
than in acetonitrile. A good compromise was to use a mixture
of CH
3CN and DMF (1:1). In these conditions, the α-AAP 4 was
reduced to the α-AAllylP 5 with a good yield (68 %) without
any traces of other organophosphorus by-products.
We propose the following mechanism for the formation of
the α-AAllylP 5. The addition of the first electron to α-AAP 4
provides the radical-anion 6, which is protonated to form the
radical 7. Then a /betatwo-fragmentation takes place to cleave the N-
Tosyl bond, generating the imine 8 and releasing the Ts radi-
cal.[25–28] The reduction of the imine 8 gives the new radical-
anion 9 which is next protonated to give radical 10. The latter
is then reduced to the anion 11, which is protonated to provide
the desired α-AAllylP 5. In this reduction a fourth election is
needed to reduce the Ts radical generated earlier (Scheme 2).
Scheme 2. Proposed mechanism for the reduction of the
α-AAP 4 to the α-AAllylP 5.
To confirm the formation of the radical 7, leading to the
cleavage of the N–Ts bond, we extended the scope of this re-
duction to other protecting groups on the nitrogen atom. Re-
placing the tosyl group with a para-methoxybenzene sulfonyl
group led to the same type of cleavage and the resulting
α-AAllylP 12 was formed in 55 % yield. However, in the same
conditions the α-AAP protected with a mesyl group gave the
protected α-AAllylP 13 in 56 % yield. In that case, only 2 F/mol
and 2 equiv. of diethyl malonate were needed for this reduc-
tion. To force the cleavage of the N-Ms bond and to obtain the
unprotected α-AAllylP 5, instead of the protected α-AAllylP 13,
we applied a more negative potential for the reduction of the
corresponding allene, successively at –2.50 V, –2.70 V and
–2.90 V. In that case (–2.70 V and –2.90 V), we observed the
formation of 5 as the minor product of this reaction and the
formation of 13 as the major product. In both cases, the relative

proportion of 5 vs. 13 is equal to 1:2. The reduction of the
Boc-protected allenylphosphonate proceeds at a more negative
potential (–2.70 V vs. SCE) and gives the corresponding
α-AAllylP 14 in a high yield (77 %). Finally, the α-AAP protected
as a phosphoramidate was reduced in the same conditions
as the Boc-protected α-AAP (–2.70 V vs. SCE) to provide the α-
AAllylP 15 in a high yield (83 %) (Scheme 3).
Scheme 3. Study on the effect of the protecting group on the nitrogen atom.
(a) Reduction at –2.70 V vs. SCE. (b) Reduction in pure acetonitrile at –2.70 V
vs. SCE without diethyl malonate.
Interested by the α-AAllylP 5, and using our optimised condi-
tions {Et 4NBF4 [0.1 M in CH 3CN/DMF (1:1)], diethyl malonate
(4.5 equiv.), 4 F/mol, –2.50 V, r.t.}, we next explored the scope
and limitations for this reduction starting from the correspond-
ing N-Tosyl α-AAP to give the resulting α-amino allylphosphon-
ates 16–27 in moderate to excellent yields (Scheme 4).
By changing the nature of the alkyl group on the phosphon-
ate moiety, we did not observe any significant shift of the re-
duction wave and therefore the applied potential for the con-
version of the allenylphosphonates was kept at –2.50 V vs. SCE.
The corresponding α-AAllyPs 5, 16 and 17 were obtained in
good yields (Scheme 4). The obtained yield for the formation
of the α-AAllyP 5 in CH
3CN/DMF is higher than in pure CH 3CN
(see Table 1). Changing one of the alkyl groups of the phos-
phonate moiety on the α-AAP 4 with a phenyl group gives after
reduction (–2.50 V vs. SCE) the α-AAllylP 18, in 21 % yield, as a
1:1 mixture of two inseparable diastereoisomers. The low yield
observed for the formation of the α-AAllylP 18 is explained by
the instability of the latter that decomposes during purification.
Despite all of our efforts, the α-AAP 4, with two phenyl groups
on the phosphonate moiety, could not be prepared to explore
its reduction to the corresponding α-AAllylP . The effect of the
substitution on the allene moiety for this reduction was studied
first by introducing only one methyl group in order to form the
α-AAllylP 19. In that case, we observed the formation of multi-
ple products and the expected α-AAllylP 19 was isolated in a
low yield (20 %) in a 1:1 mixture of isomers. This low yield is
explained by the isomerisation of alkene to form the amino
vinylphosphonate that later decomposed during the purifica-
tion step. Next, we turned our attention to the reduction of
non-substituted α-amino allenylphosphonates. The decomposi-
tion of the α-AAllylP 20 could be explained by the isomerisation
of the carbon–carbon double bond to form the corresponding

α-amino vinylphosphonate. The latter is next decomposed lead-
ing to the formation of a pyruvate analogue. [29] In order to pre-
vent this decomposition and based on our previous results with
the Boc group, we tried to prepare the Boc-protected α-AAllylP
21. However, the latter is decomposed under the reaction con-
ditions. This result led us to continue to explore the scope of
the reduction of the α-AAP 1 (R = Ts) bearing two substituents
on the allene moiety. With identical substituents on the allene
moiety, the corresponding α-AAllylPs 22–23 were formed in
good yields. With different substituents on the allene moiety,
we observed the formation of 24, 26 and 27 in a 1:1 insepara-
ble mixture of isomers. It is noteworthy that neither the size
nor the electronic effects induced by the substituents could
influence the stereoselectivity of the reduction (Scheme 4). The
formation of the α-AAllylP 25 from the corresponding α-AAP
4a was more complicated due to the presence of the aromatic
ring on the allenyl moiety. In that case, the reduction potential
was less negative (–2.40 V vs. SCE) due to the presence of
multiple reduction waves on the starting material (see support-
ing information). However, despite that modification, the

α-AAllylP 25 was isolated in a low yield (12 %) ( E/Z = 9:1 in
favour of the E isomer) as an inseparable mixture of isomers. In
this reduction, the major product is the allylphosphonate 25′
that is isolated in a high yield (72 %) as a 9:1 mixture of isomers
in favour of the E isomer (Scheme 5). Changing the reduction
potential to –2.30 V vs. SCE did not modify the ratio of the
products formed in this reaction.

phonate 25′.
Next, we turned our attention to the substitution on the
nitrogen atom. Replacing the PMB group by an ortho-methoxy-
benzyl group led to the α-AAllylP 28 in a good yield (61 %)
with an incomplete conversion of 81 %. On the other hand,
alkenyl and alkyl substituents led respectively to the α-AAllylP
29 and 30 in a lower yield (47 % and 61 % respectively) partially
explained by the incomplete conversion of the starting material
(81 %) in the case of compound 29. Increasing or decreasing
the electron density on the aromatic ring was next explored to
prepare the α-AAllylP 31 and 32 in moderate yields. We pre-
pared the α-AAllylP 33 in a high yield (78 %) (Scheme 6). It has
to be noted that in this case the reduction potential was set to
–2.42 V vs. SCE due to the presence of a phenyl group on the
nitrogen atom that anodically shifts the reduction wave of the
corresponding α-AAP (see cyclic voltammogram in the Support-

ing Information). Finally, the compatibility of the silyl ether
functionality, in these reaction conditions, was tested for the
preparation of the α-AAllylP 34. The latter was obtained in
moderate yield (53 %) (Scheme 6).
Conclusion
In conclusion, we have prepared a series of α-amino allylphos-
phonates through the reductive electrolysis of α-amino allenyl-
phosphonates. This process is chemoselective for the formation
of the allylphosphonates. Indeed, on the studied examples, no
traces of vinyl or alkylphosphonates were observed after the
reduction. In the case of α-amino allylphosphonates protected
with a tosyl group, the latter is cleaved in the process. However,
other protecting groups (mesylate, carbamate and phosphor-
amidate) have been successfully used to prepare the corre-
sponding protected α-amino allylphosphonates. Moreover, with
this new methodology in hand we now have access, from the
same starting material (the α-amino allenylphosphonates) to
either the α-amino vinylphosphonates as described in our pre-
vious work
[8] or the α-amino allylphosphonates, as presented
herein.
Experimental Section
All reactions were carried out under argon with magnetic stirring.
All solvents and chemicals were purified based on standard proce-
dures. Reagent grade solvents were used without purification for
all extractions and work-up procedures. R
f values refer to values
obtained by TLC on 0.25 mm silica gel plates (60 F254). Flash chro-
matography was carried out on silica gel 60 (35–70 μm) with vari-
ous mixtures of ethyl acetate (EtOAc) and petroleum ether (PE),
yields refer to chromatographically and spectroscopically pure com-
pounds. All
1H, 13Ca n d 31P NMR spectra were recorded on 250,
300, 360, 400 MHz spectrometers at 300 K. Chemical shifts were
given in parts per million (ppm, δ), referenced to the solvent peak
of CDCl
3, defined at δ = 7.26 ppm ( 1H NMR) and δ = 77.16 ( 13C
NMR). HRMS spectra were recorded with a MicroTOFq spectrometer.
Electrochemical data were obtained using an EG & G 273A potentio-
stat driven by a PC with the M270 software. A divided cell with a
standard three-electrode configuration was used for cyclic voltam-
metry experiments. The referenc e electrode was a s aturated calo-
mel electrode (SCE) and the counter electrode a platinum gauze of
large surface area; both electrod es were separate d from the bulk
electrolyte solution via fritted compartments filled with the same
electrolyte, which was a solution of Et
4NBF4 (0.1 M) in a 1:1 mixture
of anhydrous DMF and anhydrous CH 3CN. The working electrode
was a ca. 120 × 10 × 2 mm 3 stick (GC, MERSEN, France) both for
cyclic voltammetry and for controlled potential coulometry experi-
ments. Prior to each experimen t, solutions were d e-aerated thor-
oughly for at least 15 min with pure Ar. A positive pressure of this
gas was maintained during subsequent work. All cyclic voltammo-
grams were recorded at a scan rate of 100 mV s
–1 unless otherwise
stated. Before the electrolysis, a cyclic voltammogram of the allene
to be reduced, mixed with the diethyl malonate, was recorded in
the same conditions as the electrolysis (same electrodes, vessels,
solvents, temperature) and is represented in the following CVs as
the blue curve. After the electrolysis, a new cyclic voltammogram
(red curve) of the reaction mixture was recorded. All experiments

General Procedure for the Electrochemical Reduction of the
α-AAP
In a divided cell, the N-Tosyl α-AAP (0.215 mmol) and diethyl
malonate (0.966 mmol, 4.5 equiv.) were added to 25 mL of a solu-
t i o no fE t
4NBF4 (0.1 M) in a 1:1 mixture of anhydrous DMF and
anhydrous CH 3CN. The solution was degassed under argon for
15 min before electrolysis. A constant potential of –2.50 V vs. SCE
(unless otherwise mentioned) was then applied at room tempera-
ture. The argon degassing was maintained during the electrolysis.
When the current was less than 5 % of its starting value, usually
after 4–5 F/mol of starting material (5 h), the electrolysis was
stopped. The solvent was removed under vacuo and the residue
was washed with EtOAc. The resulting suspension was filtered
through a pad of Celite and the so lvent was evaporated under
vacuo. The residue was purified by silica gel chromatography to
yield the expected α-AAllylP .
